concept_html:
Fabric lessons assume a shared vocabulary. Here it is, platform first, then how Fabric maps onto it.

Files and formats.

  • CSV is plain text. It stores no types, so a reader guesses them, and a postcode 01234 can come back as the number 1234.
  • Parquet stores data by column, with each column's type, and compresses it. Reading two columns of a wide table reads only those two.
  • Delta is a folder of Parquet files plus a transaction log, _delta_log. The log turns files into a table: each write is a numbered version, readers never see a half-finished write, and you can read an older version.

Places for data.

  • A data lake holds files of any shape, cheaply. Structure is applied when you read.
  • A data warehouse holds tables with a fixed schema, queried with SQL.
  • A lakehouse keeps tables in an open format, such as Delta, in a lake, so a Spark notebook and a SQL engine read the same data.

Storage and compute are separate. Data sits once in storage. Engines, such as Spark, SQL and Power BI, bring compute to it when they run.

How data moves. Batch processing handles a delivery at a time, such as a nightly file. Streaming handles events as they arrive, seconds apart. With ELT, you load raw data first, then transform it inside the platform. Many teams name the stages bronze (raw, as received), silver (cleaned) and gold (aggregated for reports).

In Fabric, all of this lives in OneLake, one logical lake for the whole organisation (GA). Lakehouse tables are Delta tables (GA). Spark reads them, and the SQL analytics endpoint (GA) queries the same tables with T-SQL. Lessons C1-L2 and C2-L1 go deeper.

reasons.text: The log tells readers which files form each version, so writes are all-or-nothing and old versions stay readable.

wrong_answers.feedback: Delta data files are ordinary Parquet files. The log beside them makes the table.
Delta stores data as Parquet, which keeps types. CSV keeps none.
Engines read Delta tables, but the table exists without any engine running.
Right part, wrong reason. Parquet does the compressing. The log records versions.

exercises.code:
import io

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"postcode": ["01234"]})
csv_text = df.to_csv(index=False)
buffer = io.BytesIO()
df.to_parquet(buffer)
buffer.seek(0)
print(pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text))["postcode"].iloc[0], pd.read_parquet(buffer)["postcode"].iloc[0])

exercises.primer:
The code uses pandas, Python's table library, and the `io` module:

- `pd.DataFrame({"postcode": ["01234"]})` builds a one-column table.
- `df.to_csv(index=False)` writes it as CSV text. `pd.read_csv(...)` reads CSV back.
- `df.to_parquet(buffer)` writes it as Parquet. `pd.read_parquet(buffer)` reads Parquet back.
- `io.StringIO(text)` and `io.BytesIO()` are in-memory stand-ins for a text file and a binary file. `buffer.seek(0)` rewinds to the start before reading.
- `["postcode"].iloc[0]` takes the first value of the column.
exercises.primer_html:

  • df.to_parquet(buffer) writes it as Parquet. pd.read_parquet(buffer) reads Parquet back.
  • io.StringIO(text) and io.BytesIO() are in-memory stand-ins for a text file and a binary file. buffer.seek(0) rewinds to the start before reading.
  • ["postcode"].iloc[0] takes the first value of the column.

exercises.model_answer:

- One typed table for several engines: Delta in a lakehouse.
- Seconds matter: streaming, not nightly batches.

recap.back: CSV: text, no types. Parquet: columnar, typed, compressed. Delta: Parquet files plus a transaction log with versions.
Lake: files, structure on read. Warehouse: typed tables for SQL. Lakehouse: open tables in a lake, read by Spark and SQL.
Load raw first, transform inside the platform: bronze (as received), silver (clean), gold (aggregated).
OneLake is the one lake (GA). Lakehouse tables are Delta (GA). The SQL analytics endpoint queries them with T-SQL (GA).

title: Data platform vocabulary, files, tables, lakes and warehouses
why_html: A team exported its gold tables to CSV for a reporting tool. Store codes such as 00042 became 42, and the join to the store list silently matched nothing for 300 stores. Reading the Delta table directly, with its types intact, avoided both the copy and the broken join.
